verses.note: Paul reads this verse against the risen Christ: the first Adam received life, the last Adam gives it (1 Corinthians 15:45). The resurrection is pictured as a new act of the creator who first breathed life into dust, and Ezekiel's valley of bones uses the same image of breath entering bodies.

The hope that God could give Isaac back from death is not stated in Genesis but drawn from it by Hebrews 11:19, which calls Isaac's return a figure of resurrection. The verse contributes a trust in God's promise that reaches past the point where death seems to end it.

Jesus appeals to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, all eventually laid in this cave, to argue that God is the God of the living (Matthew 22:31-32). The grave at Machpelah becomes part of the Bible's case for resurrection.

Jesus quotes this verse to answer the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection. God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob long after their deaths, and Jesus draws the conclusion that he is not the God of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:26-27). The covenant relationship God claims with the patriarchs, long dead when he speaks, implies that death has not ended it.

Peter argues that David died and his tomb was still in Jerusalem, so the words point beyond him to the Messiah whose body did not decay (Acts 2:29-31). The church's confession of the bodily resurrection gives the verse its fullest sense.

The psalm's turn from death's dust to praise, with the answer arriving at the last moment, became for the church the shape of Good Friday turning to Easter. Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus offered prayers with loud cries to the one able to save him from death and was heard.

After being cut off from the land of the living (verse 8) and buried (verse 9), the Servant sees offspring and prolongs his days. The song does not explain how, but it plainly speaks of life beyond his death. The New Testament reads this vindication as fulfilled in Jesus' resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3-4, according to the Scriptures).

In context the graves are the exile and the resurrection is the return. But the metaphor depends on the conviction that God can raise the dead, and it prepared the way for the explicit hope of Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.15.1) and Tertullian (On the Resurrection of the Flesh) cited this passage against those who denied the body's resurrection. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 92b) records rabbis debating whether the dead of Ezekiel's valley were actually raised, one sage calling the vision a parable and others insisting it happened.
Mark's verb ‘raised’ quietly anticipates later scenes. Jesus raises the sick, raises Jairus's daughter (5:41-42), and is himself raised (16:6).

The verse joins identity and event: the same Jesus of Nazareth who was crucified has been raised, and the place where his body lay is empty. The church's confession of Christ's bodily resurrection rests on exactly this pairing, the continuity of the person and the reality of the body.

The risen Jesus has flesh and bones and bears the marks of the cross. The church's confession of the resurrection of the body rests on this continuity: the one who was crucified is raised in the same body, now transformed, not replaced by a spirit.

The resurrection is not added to the suffering as a happy ending; both belong to what is written. Paul's early creed has the same pair and the same reference to Scripture: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).
The resurrection is God's act (‘God raised’) and God's verdict on the one the court condemned. Death's hold on Jesus is described as something that could not last.

The psalm's hope that God would not abandon his faithful one to the grave is read as a promise of bodily resurrection: not escape from death but rescue from its decay. Peter's argument is about the body in the tomb.
The resurrection is presented as an event with witnesses, not as a private experience or a symbol. The apostles' authority in Acts rests on their being witnesses of it (1:22).

The resurrection is the public act by which God installs his Son in power. It is also, by Paul's phrasing, the beginning of the resurrection of the dead: what happened to Jesus is the first fruits of what will happen to his people (1 Corinthians 15:20).
God gives life to the dead: Abraham trusted this about God before the resurrection of Jesus revealed it fully. The same God acted in Isaac's birth from a ‘dead’ body and womb and in raising Jesus.

The resurrection is not an afterthought to justification. It is God's public vindication of the one who died for sinners, and so the declaration that his death has done its work; justification is bound to the risen Christ.

Christ's resurrection is here both the pattern and the power for believers' present life. Paul holds back from saying believers have already been raised (contrast Colossians 2:12 and Ephesians 2:6); in Romans the full share in resurrection is still future (verse 5, 8:11), while its life already shapes how they walk.

Christ ‘cannot die again’: his resurrection is the start of the life of the age to come, not a temporary restoration. That quality of life is what believers are joined to, which is why their hope is secure.

The verse promises the resurrection of believers' bodies, raised by the same God and through the same Spirit who raised Jesus. Christian hope is embodied: God will give life to mortal bodies, not release souls from them.
The final stage of adoption is the body's redemption at the resurrection. Paul's hope for the body is not escape from it but its release from mortality.

The creed places burial between death and raising. That order is why the church has confessed a bodily resurrection: what was raised is what was buried, not a spirit that survived apart from the body.

Paul treats the resurrection as an event with public witnesses who could be questioned, not a private conviction. The Christian claim is historical in form, and the apostle invites scrutiny rather than avoiding it.

The appearance to James is a strong piece of evidence in the historical case for the resurrection: a skeptical brother became a leader of the movement and died for it. Paul does not argue this, but the list places him among those who saw.
Paul will not let Christ's resurrection be treated as a unique exception. The resurrection of Jesus is the first instance of a general resurrection, so to deny the general is to deny the particular.

The resurrection is presented as an act of God: ‘He raised Christ from the dead.’ The New Testament regularly credits the raising to the Father (Acts 2:24, Romans 10:9, Galatians 1:1), and the resurrection is his public vindication of Jesus.

Christ's resurrection is not a private exception but the first part of the one resurrection of the dead. The end-time event Israel hoped for (Daniel 12:2) has begun in the middle of history with one man.

The seed image holds together continuity and change: what is sown is the same thing that grows, and yet what grows is far greater. Death is not an obstacle to resurrection but the condition through which it comes.

The same body is sown and raised, and yet it is raised in a new condition: incorruptible, glorious, powerful. Christian teaching on the resurrection holds both identity (it is this body) and transformation (it is not this body as it is now).

A ‘spiritual body’ is not a spirit instead of a body. The contrast is between the present body, suited to ordinary mortal life, and the resurrection body, wholly suited to and animated by the Spirit of God. The church has rejected readings that make the resurrection body a mere phantom.

Immortality in Paul is not a property the soul already has but a garment God gives at the resurrection. God alone has immortality by nature (1 Timothy 6:16); humans receive it as a gift, and they receive it in the body.

The resurrection is the measure of God's power toward believers. The same power that raised Christ is at work in those who believe, which Ephesians 2:5-6 will apply to their being raised and seated with him.
Christ is the firstborn from the dead, the first to rise into the life of the age to come. The title implies others will follow, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 with the image of firstfruits.
The resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment belong to the ABCs of the faith, shared ground with Pharisaic Judaism. The letter assumes them as the horizon of everything else (9:27, 11:35).

The contrast between dying priests and the one who ‘lives’ prepares for verse 16. Melchizedek lives only in the sense that Scripture records no death; Jesus lives in fact, by the power of an indestructible life, because he rose.
Jesus holds his priesthood by the power of an indestructible life. The resurrection is not only vindication; it is the ground of his continuing office, since only a living priest can serve ‘forever’.

Premillennial readers take ‘came to life’ as bodily resurrection at Christ's return, the same kind of event as the resurrection of ‘the rest of the dead’ in verse 5, which they place a thousand years later. Either way, the verse insists that those the beast killed are not finally dead.

John 5:24-29 speaks of two ‘hours’: one that ‘now is’, when the spiritually dead hear the Son's voice and live, and one that is coming, when all in the tombs will come out. Amillennial readers find the same two stages here; premillennial readers see two bodily resurrections separated by the millennium. Both read the verse as a promise that death does not have the last word over the faithful.

The verse assumes a general resurrection: those lost at sea, with no grave, and those held by Death and Hades are all restored to stand before God. The church's creeds confess the same, the resurrection of the dead and the judgment of the living and the dead.
